The Norwegian letter continues the medieval Danish–Norwegian letter ⟨ø⟩, ultimately developed from the Latin ligature ⟨œ⟩, formed by joining ⟨o⟩ and ⟨e⟩.
In medieval Scandinavian writing, the ligature developed into forms consisting of an ⟨o⟩ crossed by a horizontal, vertical or diagonal stroke. It was used to represent front rounded vowels which had developed in North Germanic, especially through i-umlaut of earlier back rounded vowels.

55437.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse sól (“sun”), from Proto-Germanic *sōl (“sun”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”). The exact inflectional prehistory of the Proto-Germanic form is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk sol, Danish sol, Swedish sol, Icelandic sól, Faroese sól, Latin sōl (“sun”) and English sun. / Borrowed from Italian sol (“sol, fifth note of the scale”), from the first syllable of Latin solve (“release, unbind”) in the medieval hymn Ut queant laxis. The note name belongs to the solmization system associated with Guido of Arezzo. / Shortened from Latin solūtiō (“solution”) (genitive solūtiōnis), originally used as an element in terms such as aerosol.
Compare German Sol, English sol and French sol (“colloidal solution”). / Clipping of solarium (“solarium, tanning bed”).

22669.etyen:
Borrowed from German Hebräer (“Hebrew”), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos, “Hebrew, Jew”), probably through Aramaic Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”), from Biblical Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrî, “Hebrew”). The origin of the Hebrew ethnonym is uncertain. It is traditionally connected with עֵבֶר (ʿēḇer, “the other side, beyond”), perhaps in the sense “one from the other side [of the river]”; a proposed connection with the ancient Near Eastern term Habiru is disputed.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk hebrear, Danish hebræer, Swedish hebré and English Hebrew (“member of the Hebrew people”).

1000077.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Chichewa Maláŵi (“Malawi”). The immediate transmission route into Norwegian is unknown.
The name is traditionally explained from Chichewa malaŵí (“flames”). In Chewa oral tradition, Malawi was the name of an area around the lake, which was said to resemble flames or a mirage when viewed from the surrounding highlands. Early Portuguese sources rendered the name as Maravj or Maravy, whence the conventional name Maravi for the precolonial state in the region. The modern country adopted the name Malawi when it became independent in 1964, replacing the colonial name Nyasa

1000333.etyen:
Internationalism; borrowed from Latin Eurōpa, from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē), used in Ancient Greek both as a geographical name and as the name of a mythological figure. The ultimate origin is uncertain and probably Pre-Greek. The geographical and mythological uses may ultimately represent the same name, but a direct historical connection between them has not been established. The traditional interpretation of the mythological name as εὐρύς (eurús, “wide, broad”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, face”) is uncertain, as are proposed connections with Semitic words meaning “evening” or “west”.
Compare Danish

1001357.etyen:
A spelling variant of Kasper, corresponding to Danish and Swedish Casper and Casper. Ultimately from Medieval Latin Caspar, traditionally the name of one of the Magi in Western Christianity. The name is usually explained as ultimately deriving from an Old Persian title meaning “treasurer”, though the precise historical transmission into the medieval personal name is uncertain.
The spelling Casper has an established Norwegian history and was used in Norway in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, before becoming substantially more popular from the late twentieth century.
Compare Danish Caspe

1001613.etyen:
From Johan (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Johan”. The given name Johan is a German short form of Johannes, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
Compare Danish Johansen, Swedish Johansson, Icelandic Jóhannsson, German Johannsen and English Johnson (“patronymic surnames”).
